sections.h2: Where Wayne County tax business happens
sections.html:
Tax matters run through 428 West Liberty Street in Wooster, where the Auditor, the Treasurer and the Board of Revision share an address. The Auditor counts about 59,000 parcels, so the Treasurer mails a very large number of bills twice a year.

Ownership runs high in the county. About 76.6 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, and the typical owner-held home is valued at $222,100. That is the price range most Wayne County sellers are working in.

sections.h2: How a Wayne County tax bill is put together
sections.html:
Each parcel is taxed on 35 percent of market value. Multiply that taxable figure by the rate for your district, then subtract the reduction factor that keeps voted levies at the revenue voters approved.

  • A rollback credit from 1971 applies to most residential parcels.
  • A separate credit helps owner-occupied homes, covering the dwelling and up to one acre of home site.
  • County millage pays for the general fund, children services, the County Care Center, Medway Drug Enforcement and the board of developmental disabilities.
  • Libraries, fire districts and Wayne Holmes Mental Health fall under "Other" on the distribution panel, next to township, city and school levies.

Unvoted millage stops at 10 mills under Ohio law. A chart of districts and rates sits on the Treasurer's tax information page.

Bills arrive in two installments. January or February brings the first, June or July the second, and each bill prints its own due date.

Wayne County collection schedule
InstallmentBills issuedLast day at banksLast day at the Treasurer
First halfJanuary or FebruaryEarly FebruaryLate February
Second halfJune or JulyMid-JulyLate July

Past the due date, a 10 percent penalty is added, and half is given back if the balance is cleared inside 10 days. Cards and mobile wallets work through Autoagent for a 2.35 percent fee with a $2.00 floor. The e-check fee is $0.50, and a bounced check costs $15.00. Postmarks count on mailed payments, but a postmark can trail the day you mailed, and the September delinquent cycle accepts none.

If nothing is in your mailbox by July 1, call 330-287-5450. State law at R.C. 323.13 treats a missing bill as no excuse for paying late.

Disputes go to the Board of Revision through the Auditor. The window opens January 1 and closes March 31, subject to the later-date rule in R.C. 5715.19. For tax year 2026 the Auditor lists January 1, 2027 to March 31, 2027.

  • Sign the complaint before a notary. Auditor staff will usually notarize it at the counter.
  • Postmark mail by March 31. Send email or fax before 11:59 pm that night.
  • Expect one complaint per three-year cycle, with exceptions for an arm's length sale, casualty loss, major improvement or a 15 percent occupancy swing.
  • Keep paying the first half bill. The second half bill waits until the Board rules, then reflects the difference.

Call the Board of Revision at 330-287-5433 with questions about your complaint.

Three programs sit with the Auditor: the homestead exemption, the owner-occupied credit and current agricultural use value. The forms library lists DTE 105A (homestead application), 105B (continuing application), 105C (owner-occupancy credit), 105E (disability certificate) and 105I (owners with a service-related disability and surviving spouses).

Exemption applications for churches, schools, nonprofits and public land are filed there too. Age and income limits shift between tax years, so call the real estate division at 330-287-5430 for the numbers that apply to you before counting on a credit.

sections.h2: At the Auditor's counter when a house sells
sections.html:
The deed makes a short trip inside one building: Map Office, then Auditor, then Recorder. Four dollars per thousand of price is the conveyance rate, with 50 cents per parcel on top, and the price is rounded up to the next $100.

  • Recording costs $34.00 for two pages and $8.00 per extra page.
  • A grantee's value statement under R.C. 319.202 must precede the Auditor's endorsement.
  • Online tools include a conveyance calculator, a tax estimator and a levy estimator.

Settle tax proration in the contract, and get a payoff from the Treasurer for any parcel carrying a balance. The delinquent list on the Treasurer's site shows parcels with unpaid years.

sections.h2: The six-year reappraisal and your value
sections.html:
Ohio requires the Auditor to run a countywide reappraisal every six years. Once the state approves a final abstract of values, new tax rates for the next tax year follow from those values, the levies voters passed and the 10 mills receivable by the county. If values climb, the state applies reduction factors so a levy cannot raise more than the amount first voted.

The county's 2026 reappraisal opens the three-year cycle that the one-complaint rule above refers to. Look up your parcel on the Auditor's site to find the proposed value before you set an asking price, and call the Auditor if the number looks off.

Some categories can be exempt: the actual place of worship and its fellowship halls (a parsonage is not exempt), schools and their athletic facilities, townships, cities and villages, county land, public parks, state property, colleges, graveyards, hospitals and nonprofits such as the Salvation Army. Land leased out for profit, or vacant with no planned use, does not qualify.

  • Community Reinvestment Area abatements are available only where a city, village or county has had an area approved by the state development agency.
  • Tax increment financing diverts part of the tax on added value to the municipality or to a city and school combination.
  • Manufactured homes are billed on a separate duplicate. The tax base is 40 percent of depreciated value under the older rule, and a 1998 law moved new assessments toward market value.

Start with a payoff from the Treasurer at 330-287-5450. Tell the title company about any unpaid year so it can be paid from your proceeds at closing. A cash buyer skips the lender's escrow check, but the title search still finds a balance, so clearing it early keeps the closing on schedule. Put the proration of the current year in the contract in writing.

Here is a short order of work. Pull your latest bill and note which half is still unpaid. Call the Treasurer for the payoff figure. Ask the title company whether it will pay the balance from your proceeds. Keep the proration language in the contract so the buyer and you agree on who covers which months. If the bill is late, ask whether the penalty can be reduced by paying inside the grace window.

faqs.q: When are Wayne County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due in late February and the second half in late July, with earlier cutoffs for payments made at banks. Every bill prints its own deadline.

faqs.q: How long does a Wayne County owner have to contest a valuation?
faqs.a: From January 1 through March 31. For tax year 2026 the window is January 1, 2027 to March 31, 2027, and mailed complaints need a March 31 postmark.

faqs.q: What does the Wayne County Auditor charge on a deed?
faqs.a: Four dollars per $1,000 of price plus $0.50 per parcel, with price rounded up to the next $100. The Auditor's calculator does the arithmetic.

faqs.q: Does the Wayne County Treasurer accept cards?
faqs.a: Yes, including Apple Pay, Google Pay and Samsung Pay, online, at 1-844-615-1900 or at the office. Expect a 2.35 percent charge with a $2.00 floor, or $0.50 by e-check.

faqs.q: Where do I file a deed after closing in Wayne County?
faqs.a: With the Recorder on the first floor of 428 West Liberty Street in Wooster, 330-287-5460, once the Auditor has endorsed it. Deeds, mortgages, liens and plats are filed there.
